claims.claim: Evagrius Ponticus was a Christian mystic and writer who lived from approximately 345 to 399 CE.
Evagrius was born in Ibora, Pontus, and died in Cellia, Nitrian Desert, Egypt.
Evagrius was ordained a reader by Basil of Caesarea and later served as archdeacon under Gregory of Nazianzus in Constantinople, where he participated in the Second Ecumenical Council in 381.

After a personal spiritual crisis, Evagrius left Constantinople for Jerusalem around 382, where he joined the monastic communities of Melania the Elder and Rufinus of Aquileia, taking monastic vows in 383.
Evagrius then traveled to Egypt, where he spent the rest of his life in the monasteries of Nitria and Kellia, studying, teaching, and writing on the ascetic life until his death in 399.

The Institutio sive Paraenesis ad monachos, also known as Counsel to Monks or Exhortations to Monks, is a text of 58 chapters in two sections (of 16 and 42 chapters, after longer and shorter recensions are collated).
The chapters are generally proverbial admonitions to monks regarding the life of virtue and combat with evil thoughts.

The work has no defined systematic plan, but contains loose groupings of sentences around individual themes, with the first part covering vices and purification and the second focusing on trials, temptations, faithfulness to Trinitarian doctrine, and warnings to sinners.
Evagrius developed a meticulous taxonomy of evil thoughts, their origins, and the physical experiences associated with them, arranging his works in an ascetic curriculum for the training of monks.

Evagrius's theology of contemplative prayer and asceticism laid the groundwork for a tradition of spiritual life in both Eastern and Western churches, though his teachings were later considered unorthodox in some strands of Christianity.
